title: Ultimate Positivity problem
formal: Does there exist a single deterministic Turing machine which, for every finite description of a rational linear recurrence sequence \((u_n)_{n\ge0}\), halts and correctly decides whether \[\exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\ge N,\qquad u_n\ge0?\] The input consists of \(k\ge1\), rational coefficients \(a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\), and rational initial terms \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\); subsequent terms satisfy \[u_{n+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}a_j u_{n+j}\qquad(n\ge0).\] The supplied recurrence length \(k\) is unrestricted, and repeated characteristic roots are allowed. “Positivity” in this problem's established name means nonnegativity.
why: Ultimate Positivity asks whether finitely specified linear dynamics eventually remain on one side of a boundary. It connects recurrence sequences, eventual program behavior and precise approximation questions in number theory. A resolution would determine whether eventual sign stability is algorithmically recognizable even when repeated roots introduce polynomial factors and several oscillating contributions interact.
status_note: Explicitly open in the termination survey version of 24 July 2026, p. 26. The checked positive results cover general recurrences through order five and simple recurrences at arbitrary order; the May 2026 preprint has a unique-dominant-root restriction. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 found no matching general resolution. This records the dated literature evidence and model checks, not an exhaustive status guarantee or independent formal verification of cited proofs.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-16; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: The source traces the general Positivity and Ultimate Positivity decision questions to the formal-language and recurrence literature of the 1970s.
The low-order theorem decides Ultimate Positivity through order five; its Theorem 7 identifies the Diophantine computability consequence of an order-six algorithm.
Ultimate Positivity becomes decidable for simple recurrences of every order, in polynomial space overall and polynomial time at each fixed order. The procedure does not generally compute a threshold.
The checked unique-dominant-root preprint gives sufficient conditions for a restricted spectral setting. It does not claim general decidability for the inputs defined here.
The revised termination survey explicitly describes unrestricted Ultimate Positivity as an open problem, with general decidability known through order five.

importance.reason: A longstanding central decision problem for linear recurrences with direct verification interpretations and a proved order-six connection to difficult Diophantine approximation. It is distinct from all-time positivity and remains unresolved beyond the known general low-order boundary in the checked July 2026 survey.

sentences: A rational linear recurrence describes an infinite sequence using finitely many initial terms and constant coefficients.
Ultimate Positivity asks whether every sufficiently late term is nonnegative, allowing a finite negative prefix and infinitely many zero terms.
The target is one uniform decision procedure for arbitrary recurrence lengths, including repeated characteristic roots.
The general problem is decidable through order five and the simple-root subclass is decidable at every order, while the July 2026 survey retains the unrestricted problem as open.
Its resolution would connect algorithmic eventual sign analysis with central questions about linear dynamics and Diophantine approximation.

definitions: Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Each rational input is encoded exactly as a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. The lists and their lengths are explicit finite input; the recurrence coefficients are constant in \(n\). These data uniquely determine every rational term. The supplied recurrence need not have minimum possible length. Its characteristic polynomial is \(p(X)=X^k-\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}a_jX^j\); no restriction is imposed on its roots, their multiplicities, ratios or moduli. In particular, zero coefficients and zero roots are allowed. A sequence is ultimately nonnegative exactly when the set \(\{n\in\mathbb N:u_n<0\}\) is finite. Infinitely many zeros are permitted, and the identically zero sequence is a yes-instance. A no-instance has \(\forall N\in\mathbb N\ \exists n\ge N:u_n<0\). The decision algorithm must be uniform in all recurrence lengths, coefficients and initial values, must use no oracle, and must always give the exact correct answer; there is no error probability, numerical tolerance, or time bound. Invalid encodings may be rejected. No threshold needs to be included with a yes-answer. Rational rather than integer data do not change this decidability target: for a positive integer \(D\) divisible by all input denominators, \(v_n=D^{n+1}u_n\) has integer initial terms, integer recurrence coefficients \(a_jD^{k-j}\), and exactly the same signs.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of decidability or undecidability for the exact input language above. A positive answer must establish one total computable yes/no procedure correct for all finite recurrence descriptions. A negative answer must prove that no such procedure exists. Resolving an arbitrary fixed low order or the simple-root subclass positively is only partial; an undecidability theorem for any contained subclass would suffice negatively. A yes-answer is allowed without producing a threshold, because the target is the decision problem itself.

source_formulation.text: Given a rational linear recurrence sequence, decide whether all but finitely many of its terms are nonnegative, with no bound on the recurrence order.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question

context_blocks.text: A finite recurrence description controls an infinite sequence. Eventual nonnegativity allows a finite exceptional prefix: \(u_n=n-5\) satisfies a constant-coefficient recurrence and is a yes-instance even though its first five terms are negative. In contrast, \(u_n=(-1)^n\) has arbitrarily late negative terms. The sequence need not converge or increase, and zeros can continue forever.

The question differs from requiring every term to be nonnegative, which is the Positivity problem, and from asking whether some term is zero, which is the Skolem problem. These problems share the same input format but have different quantifiers. The general Ultimate Positivity target includes repeated characteristic roots; it is not replaced by the already decidable simple-root subclass.

Ouaknine and Worrell prove a polynomial-time decision procedure for Ultimate Positivity when the recurrence has order at most five. At order six they prove a number-theoretic implication: decidability would make a specified family of Diophantine-approximation constants computable. This is a conditional consequence of a decision procedure, not a proof of undecidability.

For simple recurrences, whose minimal characteristic polynomial has distinct roots, Ultimate Positivity is decidable at every order. The known procedure can return yes without providing an index after which every term is nonnegative. Computing such an index is a separate effective-threshold problem, retained in the related card.

The July 2026 termination survey still identifies unrestricted Ultimate Positivity as open. Its algorithm for termination from all integer initial states does not decide the eventual sign behavior of one supplied sequence; those quantifiers lead to different questions. This is recent explicit source evidence, with the usual limit that a literature check is not a proof that no later result exists.

The May 2026 preprint on arbitrary-order polynomial-coefficient recurrences gives sufficient conditions with a unique dominant root. Arbitrary order alone does not supply a solution to this card: the present input permits repeated roots and multiple roots of maximal modulus and requires a total decision procedure for every instance.
